analysis.one_liner: Fully funds federal school aid for disadvantaged students and students with disabilities.
analysis.headline: A bill with 65 cosponsors from both parties to fully fund Title I and special-education aid never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Keep Our PACT Act would put federal school funding into the law itself rather than leaving it to the yearly budget fight. It would raise Title I aid — money for schools serving low-income students — from about $17.6 billion to $46.2 billion a year over ten years, and it would raise federal special-education (IDEA) aid until it covers 40 percent of the national average cost of educating a student with a disability, the share Congress promised in 2004 but has never reached. The money would flow automatically, without requiring a new vote each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Students in school districts with many low-income children, students with disabilities, and the teachers and staff who serve them. School districts and state budgets also gain, because the federal government would pick up a much larger share of special-education costs that states and local property taxpayers currently cover.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income students and students with disabilities

how_it_helps.text: The bill would raise annual Title I funding for schools serving disadvantaged students on a fixed schedule, reaching $46,191,622,000 by fiscal year 2029.

It would raise federal special-education aid under IDEA in yearly steps until it reaches $43,312,845,000, or 40 percent of the national average per-pupil spending, by fiscal year 2029 and every year after — the 40 percent share Congress committed to in the 2004 IDEA reauthorization but never funded.
The money would be appropriated directly by the bill itself for fiscal years 2020 through 2029, rather than depending on the annual appropriations process.
The CRS summary describes the bill as providing funding for disadvantaged students under the ESEA and reauthorizing IDEA support for states and outlying areas serving children with disabilities.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. The bill authorizes roughly $46 billion a year for Title I and more than $43 billion a year for IDEA by the end of the decade, a large increase over current levels, and includes no tax or revenue offset to pay for it.

drawbacks.text: The cost is very large: the schedules in the bill add tens of billions of dollars in new federal spending each year, and the bill contains no revenue source or offset.
Because the funding is mandatory, future Congresses could not adjust it through the regular yearly budget process, reducing flexibility if enrollment or needs change.

A fair objection from the other side: sending more money to schools does not by itself guarantee better results, and critics argue states should keep more control over how education dollars are spent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: Title I and IDEA shortfalls fall hardest on low-income districts and on children with disabilities, and local school budgets have carried those costs for decades. The drawback is honest and substantial — this is a major spending increase with no offset, and putting it on autopilot trades flexibility for predictability. On balance it is a straightforward transfer to public schools, not a hidden giveaway, and the phase-in spreads the cost over a decade.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled a hearing or a vote, and it died there when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Susie Lee of Nevada introduced the bill on April 12, 2019, with 16 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day.
Sixty-five House members cosponsored the bill — 63 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The full action history shows no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action after the referral; the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No company or industry gained. The federal Treasury kept the roughly tens of billions a year it would otherwise have sent to schools, and state and local taxpayers kept carrying special-education costs that Congress promised in 2004 to cover but never did.

for.name: Rep. Susie Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to fully fund Title I and IDEA and recruited 16 original cosponsors.

for.name: National Education Association
for.what_they_did: Ran a public campaign for Congress to fund the 40 percent special-education promise and the Title I commitment.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill's last action was the referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — 63 Democrats and 2 Republicans signed on — but because the bill never got a hearing or a vote, there is no record of who opposed it.

industries.note: Districts would receive sharply higher federal Title I and special-education funding, letting them serve low-income students and children with disabilities while easing pressure on local budgets. No industry stands opposite this benefit; the cost falls on federal taxpayers generally.

industries.industry: State governments and local property taxpayers
industries.note: States and local districts currently cover most special-education costs because federal IDEA aid falls far short of the promised 40 percent; full funding would shift that burden to Washington.
